newsitem.title: GERMANY: OECD sees pan-German growth at 2.2 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees pan-German growth at 2.2 pct in 1997.

text.p: The German economy will expand by 2.2 percent in 1997, accelerating to 2.8 percent in 1998, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said on Tuesday.

In a report completed on July 8, the Paris-based forecasting unit said: "The momentum given by exports should ensure the continuation of a moderate upswing during 1997 and 1998....Higher export growth is projected to stimulate a recovery in investment in machinery and equipment."
The German economy grew just 1.4 percent in 1996.
But the think-tank warned that private consumption was likely to remain weak, at least in 1997, while unemployment would stay strong.

"Consumption will expand only modestly in 1997, restrained by cuts in benefit programmes and an increase in social security charges, as well as a lack of confidence in view of adverse labour market conditions," it said.

It predicted that Germany would register about 4.3 million unemployed in 1997 and 4.2 million in 1998, up from 4.0 million in 1996. The unemployment rate would rise from 1996's 10.3 percent to 11.1 percent in 1997 before easing to 10.9 in 1998.
Current monetary and exchange rate conditions were nonetheless supportive for faster growth, the OECD said.

"In real terms, short-term rates of interest are at a twenty-year low. Long-term rates, although volatile, have come down significantly in relation to the dollar rates and this has been associated with a substantial depreciation of the deutschemark against the dollar since mid-1995.
"This exchange-rate adjustment has been the most important factor contributing to financial conditions which appear to be favourable to business growth," the OECD said.
The forecasting unit also stressed the need for continued reform to address structural problems and outmoded regulations.
"To achieve durable gains in the reduction of unemployment will require greater progress than has been achieved to date in the areas of labour and product market reform," it said.
"The process of reform has been made more difficult by the fact that effective consensus-based decisions have proved elusive," it added.
"Policy (must) create an institutional framework where the full benefits of European and global integration can be realised and unemployment durably and markedly lowered."
